lead: This unit teaches how symmetric encryption works, from Caesar shifts to AES and the security definitions used in proofs. After it you can trace a block cipher round, choose a mode of operation, and explain what CPA and CCA security mean.
about: The unit moves from hand ciphers to the modern definitions used for symmetric encryption. Chapter 3.1 shows substitution and transposition and why patterns break them. Chapter 3.2 states perfect secrecy and the one-time pad. Chapter 3.3 introduces pseudorandom generators and stream ciphers such as RC4. Chapters 3.4 to 3.6 build block ciphers: the Feistel structure, DES with triple DES, then AES. Chapter 3.7 explains modes that handle messages longer than one block. Chapter 3.8 covers linear and differential cryptanalysis. Chapter 3.9 closes with CPA and CCA security and pseudorandom functions, the language used for proofs and protocol design.

chapters.idea: Classical ciphers replace letters or move them, so secrecy rests on a shared rule that an attacker can often infer from patterns.
chapters.depth: Cover monoalphabetic substitution: Caesar shift and affine cipher c = (a·p + b) mod 26, with A=0, ..., Z=25; define plaintext, ciphertext, key. Cover transposition: rail fence and columnar with a keyword. Show frequency analysis and anagram patterns break them. Some syllabi call these traditional ciphers. Keep to hand examples.

figure.title: Caesar cipher on EXAM
figure.aria: A Caesar cipher shifts each letter of EXAM by three places to HADP, and shifting back recovers the message.

chapters.example: Encrypt EXAM with a Caesar shift of +3, using A=0. E→H, X→A, A→D, M→P; the ciphertext is HADP. Decrypt by shifting each letter back 3 places.
chapters.trap: Do not call Vigenère a simple substitution cipher; its key changes per letter. In transposition the letters are unchanged, only their order moves.
chapters.leave: Frequency tables for English and modern threat models are not repeated; see Unit 1 for security attacks and services.

chapters.idea: Perfect secrecy means the ciphertext gives no information about the message, and the one-time pad is the simplest cipher that reaches it.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Give Shannon's definition: Pr[M=m | C=c] = Pr[M=m] for all m,c with nonzero probability. State and prove the one-time pad c = m ⊕ k with k uniform, as long as m, used once. Show key reuse leaks m1 ⊕ m2. Mention limits: key length, key distribution, no integrity.

figure.title: One-time pad encryption and decryption
figure.aria: A message and a random key are XORed to give the ciphertext, and the same key XORed again recovers the message.

chapters.trap: The pad must be as long as the message, truly random, and never reused. A stream cipher that expands a short seed is not a one-time pad.
chapters.prereq: Basic XOR from digital logic; Chapter 3.1 for cipher notation.
chapters.leave: PRG-based stream ciphers are Chapter 3.3; message integrity is Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A pseudorandom generator stretches a short secret seed into a long keystream, and a stream cipher XORs that keystream with the message.
chapters.depth: Define PRG: deterministic G: {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1}^ℓ(n) with ℓ(n)>n; indistinguishable from random for any efficient distinguisher. Define stream cipher and nonce. Describe RC4: KSA fills a 256-byte S array, PRGA outputs keystream bytes; mention known biases and why RC4 is deprecated. Some syllabi call this an additive stream cipher.

figure.title: Stream cipher from a PRG
figure.aria: A short seed is expanded by a pseudorandom generator into a keystream, which is XORed with the plaintext to make the ciphertext.

chapters.trap: Reusing the same keystream with two messages leaks their XOR. RC4 is not secure for new systems; do not confuse a PRG with a true random generator.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.2 for one-time pad limits; basic XOR.
chapters.leave: Block ciphers are Chapter 3.4; CPA and CCA definitions are Chapter 3.9.

chapters.idea: A Feistel round mixes one half of the block into the other and swaps halves, so the same structure decrypts when subkeys are reversed.
chapters.depth: Define block size, key, round function F, and subkeys. Write one round: Lᵢ = Rᵢ₋₁, Rᵢ = Lᵢ₋₁ ⊕ F(Rᵢ₋₁, Kᵢ). Show decryption with Kᵣ...K₁. Explain confusion and diffusion. F need not be invertible. Some syllabi call this a Feistel network.

figure.title: One Feistel round
figure.aria: The right half enters the round function, its output is XORed with the left half, and the halves swap to form the next block.

chapters.example: One round: L₀ = 1010, R₀ = 0110, F(R₀,K₁) = 0011. New L₁ = R₀ = 0110. New R₁ = L₀ ⊕ F = 1010 ⊕ 0011 = 1001. Block after one round is 01101001.
chapters.trap: Do not invert F to decrypt a Feistel cipher; reverse the subkey order and run the same round. Check whether your definition swaps the halves after the last round.
chapters.leave: DES details are Chapter 3.5; AES uses a different structure in Chapter 3.6.

chapters.idea: DES applies 16 Feistel rounds with a 56-bit key to 64-bit blocks, and triple DES stretches the short key by repeated encryption.
chapters.depth: Cover initial permutation, 32-bit halves, 48-bit subkeys from a 56-bit key, eight S-boxes mapping 6 bits to 4, P-box, final permutation. Describe 3DES EDE with two or three keys and effective key sizes. Mention DES's 56-bit key is too small today. Some syllabi call 3DES TDEA.

figure.title: DES encryption flow
figure.aria: A 64-bit plaintext passes through the initial permutation, sixteen Feistel rounds using subkeys, a swap, and the inverse permutation to give the ciphertext.

chapters.example: S1 input = 011001. Row bits are first and last: 01 = 1. Column bits are middle four: 1100 = 12. S1 row 1, column 12 gives decimal 9, binary 1001.
chapters.trap: DES has a 64-bit key with 8 parity bits, so the effective key is 56 bits. 3DES with two keys gives about 112-bit strength, not 168.
chapters.leave: AES is Chapter 3.6; linear and differential attacks are Chapter 3.8.

chapters.idea: AES is a byte-oriented substitution-permutation network with 10, 12 or 14 rounds and no Feistel swap.
chapters.depth: Cover state as 4×4 bytes, AddRoundKey, SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns over GF(2⁸), and key expansion. AES-128: 10 rounds, 128-bit key; AES-192: 12; AES-256: 14. Last round omits MixColumns. Mention finite field arithmetic from Unit 2. Some syllabi call it Rijndael.

figure.title: AES round structure
figure.aria: A 128-bit plaintext enters AddRoundKey and the round steps SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey, with a dashed loop for later rounds and a final path to ciphertext.

chapters.example: AES SubBytes on byte 0x53. Look up row 5, column 3 in the AES S-box; the entry is 0xED. So SubBytes(0x53) = 0xED.
chapters.trap: AES is not a Feistel cipher. MixColumns is omitted in the final round; the key schedule is not the encryption round.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.4 for round structure; Unit 2 for GF(2⁸).
chapters.leave: Modes are Chapter 3.7; cryptanalysis is Chapter 3.8.

chapters.idea: A mode of operation turns a fixed-size block cipher into a scheme for arbitrary-length messages, using an IV or counter to vary encryption.
chapters.depth: Cover ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB, and CTR. Show padding, IV/nonce rules, error propagation, and parallelism. Define Cᵢ = E_K(Pᵢ ⊕ Cᵢ₋₁) for CBC with C₀ = IV; CTR uses E_K(nonce || counter). Explain ECB leaks equal blocks. Some syllabi call these confidentiality modes.

figure.title: CBC mode with two blocks
figure.aria: The first plaintext block is XORed with the IV and encrypted to C1; the second plaintext block is XORed with C1 and encrypted to C2, showing the chaining.

chapters.trap: ECB is not safe for multi-block messages because equal plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks. An IV is not secret but must be unique and unpredictable for CBC; a counter must never repeat under one key.
chapters.leave: MAC and CCA security are Chapter 3.9 and Unit 4; TLS modes are Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Linear cryptanalysis finds linear approximations that hold with bias; differential cryptanalysis follows input-output differences that occur with high probability, both to recover key bits.
chapters.depth: Define a linear approximation over bits: XOR of selected plaintext, ciphertext and key bits equals 0 with probability 1/2 + ε; bias is ε. Define a differential pair and characteristic probability. Show S-box table use. Mention Matsui's DES attacks and AES resistance. Keep key recovery as an outline, not a full attack.

figure.title: Differential trail through rounds
figure.aria: A chosen input difference passes through several rounds, and each round produces the next difference with a stated probability until a final output difference is reached.

chapters.example: DES S1 maps 000000 to 14 (1110) and 000001 to 0 (0000). Input difference = 000000 ⊕ 000001 = 000001. Output difference = 1110 ⊕ 0000 = 1110. This is one differential pair for the S-box.
chapters.trap: A high-probability trail does not give the key directly; it ranks key guesses. Linear bias is not the same as output difference; do not mix the two attacks.
chapters.leave: Formal security definitions are Chapter 3.9; side-channel attacks are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Modern encryption security is defined by attack games: the adversary cannot tell ciphertexts of chosen messages apart, even with chosen-ciphertext queries in CCA.
chapters.depth: Define IND-CPA and IND-CCA games and advantage. Define pseudorandom function F: K×X→Y indistinguishable from a random function, and PRP. Construct CPA-secure encryption from a PRF with a random nonce: C=(r, F_K(r)⊕m). Explain that CCA needs authenticity; encrypt-then-MAC. Mention one-way functions and hardcore predicates as related terms. Some syllabi call this semantic security.

figure.aria: The adversary asks an encryption oracle for Enc(0000), receives 1010, sends two challenge messages, receives challenge ciphertext 1010, and guesses the first message.

chapters.example: Deterministic encryption E_K(m) = m ⊕ K with K = 1010. The adversary asks Enc(0000) and gets 1010. The challenge ciphertext is 1010. If m0 = 0000 and m1 = 1111, the adversary guesses b = 0 with advantage 1. The scheme is not IND-CPA.
chapters.trap: CPA security does not allow decryption queries; CCA does. A PRF is not a PRG: a PRF takes a key and an input; a PRG takes only a seed. A random nonce is essential for the PRF construction.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.3 PRG/stream; Chapter 3.7 modes; Unit 4 MAC.
chapters.leave: Public-key CPA/CCA and zero knowledge are Unit 4; hash and MAC details are Unit 4.
